title: Job 41:25–34
context: The LORD concludes his speech. The mighty retreat before Leviathan, every weapon fails against it, it churns the deep, and it has no equal on earth, “king over all the sons of pride” (41:25–34). Job’s reply follows in 42:1–6. The poem leaves Job before creatures he cannot master and before the Creator who rules them.

verses.text: When he raises himself up, the mighty are afraid. They retreat before his thrashing.
verses.arminianNotes: “When he raises himself up, the mighty are afraid.” Arminian readers see even the strongest people retreating when Leviathan rises, showing the limits of human courage.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the mighty humbled before this creature. Readers in this tradition hear the verse as part of the LORD’s lesson that human power has its bounds.

verses.text: If one attacks him with the sword, it can’t prevail; nor the spear, the dart, nor the pointed shaft.
verses.arminianNotes: “If one attacks him with the sword, it can’t prevail; nor the spear, the dart, nor the pointed shaft.” Arminian readers see every weapon of war shown to be useless against the creature.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see human weaponry failing. Readers in this tradition note that only God can master what humans cannot, a theme echoed where Scripture pictures the LORD overcoming Leviathan (Psalm 74:14).

verses.text: He counts iron as straw, and bronze as rotten wood.
verses.arminianNotes: “He counts iron as straw, and bronze as rotten wood.” Arminian readers see the strongest human materials treated as worthless by the creature, emphasizing its invulnerability.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see human strength reduced to nothing before Leviathan. The comparison keeps the focus on how far creation exceeds human control while remaining under God’s rule.

verses.text: The arrow can’t make him flee. Sling stones are like chaff to him.
verses.arminianNotes: “The arrow can’t make him flee. Sling stones are like chaff to him.” Arminian readers see more examples of weapons failing, building a list meant to overwhelm Job with the creature’s might.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the list of weapons growing. Readers in this tradition take the cumulative effect as the point: Job cannot stand against even one of God’s creatures.

verses.text: Clubs are counted as stubble. He laughs at the rushing of the javelin.
verses.arminianNotes: “Clubs are counted as stubble. He laughs at the rushing of the javelin.” Arminian readers see the creature laughing at danger, echoing other creatures in the LORD’s speeches that scorn fear.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the creature unafraid. Readers in this tradition note similar language for the horse in 39:22, linking Leviathan to the gallery of creatures the LORD sets before Job.

verses.text: His undersides are like sharp potsherds, leaving a trail in the mud like a threshing sledge.
verses.arminianNotes: “His undersides are like sharp potsherds, leaving a trail in the mud like a threshing sledge.” Arminian readers see the creature leaving its mark wherever it moves.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a vivid picture of Leviathan’s passage. Readers in this tradition take the imagery as poetic description, not as data to be pressed for a precise identification.

verses.text: He makes the deep to boil like a pot. He makes the sea like a pot of ointment.
verses.arminianNotes: “He makes the deep to boil like a pot. He makes the sea like a pot of ointment.” Arminian readers see the creature stirring the waters, showing its power over the sea.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the sea churned by Leviathan. In Scripture the sea often stands for forces only God can rule, and readers in this tradition see the LORD’s sovereignty over even such a creature.

verses.text: He makes a path shine after him. One would think the deep had white hair.
verses.arminianNotes: “He makes a path shine after him. One would think the deep had white hair.” Arminian readers see the shining wake left behind the creature, pictured as white hair on the deep.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see beauty and power in the image. Readers in this tradition note that the LORD describes even fearsome creatures with wonder, inviting Job to share his perspective.

verses.text: On earth there is not his equal, that is made without fear.
verses.arminianNotes: “On earth there is not his equal, that is made without fear.” Arminian readers see Leviathan presented as unmatched among creatures, yet still described as something “made.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the word “made,” which keeps Leviathan within creation. However great the creature, readers in this tradition stress that it remains God’s work and under his rule.

verses.text: He sees everything that is high. He is king over all the sons of pride.”
verses.arminianNotes: “He sees everything that is high. He is king over all the sons of pride.” Arminian readers see the speech ending with Leviathan as king over the proud, a creature God alone can humble.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the climax of the speech. Readers in this tradition connect it with the LORD’s challenge to humble the proud in 40:11–12, a work that belongs to God and not to Job.
